podcast.title: Alien/God Persona
podcast.body: Following a mental crisis, English-American singer Vince Taylor believed he existed somewhere "between a god and an alien," a unique self-perception that served as inspiration for David Bowie's Ziggy Stardust character. "an English American singer, with some kind of mental crisis and now believed that he existed somewhere between a god and an alien."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Surprising History of Glam Rock

podcast.title: Covered by The Clash
podcast.body: American singer Vince Taylor's old blues song was used as a warm-up piece by The Clash during the recording sessions for their 1979 album "London Calling." Producer Guy Stevens secretly recorded the band's take on it, which he then accepted despite the band's protests about its sloppiness and tempo. "The clash went into the studio in the summer of 1979 to record what would become the London Calling album, producer Guy Stevens had all four guys warm up with a cover of an old blues song by American singer Vince Taylor."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Fabulous Style
podcast.body: Vince Taylor, as part of the Playboys, was among the artists who followed Little Richard's flamboyant path, exhibiting a distinctive and fabulous style. "Vince Taylor in the playboys... They all sounded different, but they all had a specific sort of fabulous style about them."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Teen Idol
podcast.body: He was part of a wave of teen idols who followed Tommy Steele's rise, many of whom were managed by Larry Parns. "In the wake of Steele came a whole host of other teen idols along the same lines, most of them managed by Larry Parns."

xref.title: Creation of Ziggy Stardust
xref.body: Building on glam rock concepts, Bowie developed the character Ziggy Stardust. This persona was inspired by the outrageous behavior of Iggy Pop and The Stooges, the artsy "scummy" persona of Lou Reed and the Velvet Underground, the "god-alien" self-perception of Vince Taylor, and the "space travel obsessed" persona of Norman Odom, also known as the Legendary Stardust Cowboy. Bowie combined these influences, changing "Iggy" to "Ziggy" and adopting "Stardust" as the surname. "He invented an entire character completely rooted in glam rock concepts that borrowed from the outrageous behavior of another new friend, Iggy Pop... So Bowie, taking all this information, changed Iggy to Ziggy and adopted Stardust as a surname and thus Ziggy Stardust was born."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Surprising History of Glam Rock

xref.title: Influence of Vince Taylor
xref.body: Bowie was inspired by Vince Taylor, an English-American singer who, following a mental crisis, believed himself to be an entity between a god and an alien, contributing to Ziggy's otherworldly aspect. "He'd also discovered Vince Taylor, an English American singer, with some kind of mental crisis and now believed that he existed somewhere between a god and an alien."

xref.title: Ziggy Stardust Inspiration
xref.body: David Bowie's iconic Ziggy Stardust character was partly inspired by the American singer Vince Taylor, known for his 1959 song "Brand New Cadillac." "The original was by Vince Taylor, an American singer who provided part of the inspiration for David Bowie's Ziggy Stardust character."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Ziggy Stardust Persona
xref.body: Bowie immersed himself fully into the persona of Ziggy Stardust, a "doomed pansexual alien." This character was a "pre-packaged synthetic ultra glamorous, ultra theatrical, fantastical rock star" that fundamentally changed the presentation of rock music. "Bowie immersed himself into this new persona, this doomed pansexual alien, and he invented a new name for himself. It was Ziggy Stardust."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
